summary:
Taraba State stands under Nigeria's national criminal framework. Same-sex sexual activity has been illegal there since 1904 in the Northern Region and region-wide from 1916, and the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 (SSMPA) now carries penalties of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex conduct, applicable to any person present in the country, visitors included.

The SSMPA reaches far beyond marriage. Human Rights Watch (20 October 2016) records that it bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship, and operating, participating in or supporting gay clubs, societies and organisations, with prison terms of 10 to 14 years, and that police have used it to justify torture and arbitrary arrests. The Act also criminalises attending, organising or promoting same-sex weddings and registering or publicly promoting gay groups.

Sharia application is the sharpest variable in the north. The UK Home Office country policy and information note (June 2025, updated April 2026) records that Sharia law in all twelve northern states criminalises same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions. Taraba is not named among the states that have adopted Sharia, so no Sharia application in Taraba is documented; a visitor crossing into a state that has adopted it faces exposure to those penalties.

Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public; whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here.

Trans people in Nigeria face documented killing and official indifference. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, a TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in Abuja hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; the police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing, and the Abuja police chief ordered a thorough and discreet investigation. The Dial (February 2025) records that six months after the killing no suspects had been charged.

Visitors who use dating apps face entrapment. The Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

Police violence against perceived gay people is a routine feature of enforcement. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports that Okafor, a 24-year-old man stopped by Lagos police, was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay. Those affected describe the SSMPA as a weaponised law that produces a climate of hostility independent of its text.

The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice for Nigeria, as reported by Sahara Reporters on 19 August 2026, warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, violence, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Sharia law in some northern states.

Detention carries an unresolved placement risk. Press coverage of the Bobrisky sentencing openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in, indicating that assignment between male and female sections was left to discretion rather than rule.
tangentialFactors:
Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people, and the SSMPA reinforced colonial-era criminalisation rather than introducing it.

The UK foreign office advisory reported by Sahara Reporters on 19 August 2026 also warns that mobile networks can be suspended and curfews imposed with little notice, a disruption risk that bears on reaching contacts or documenting an incident.

Human Rights Watch found that the SSMPA's passage in January 2014 was immediately followed by mob attacks, arbitrary arrests, extortion and detention of LGBT people across the country, including the arrest without charge of 21 young men at a birthday gathering in Ibadan and repeated police detentions reported by interviewees elsewhere. That national enforcement climate is the pattern against which any Taraba incident should be read, though the report names no Taraba case.
localsOnly:
Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman, pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, served in a maximum-security prison in Lagos before release on 5 August 2024. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.

Residents live with the SSMPA as an everyday instrument of extortion. Human Rights Watch interviewees describe repeated police detentions and demands for money, and the Ibadan gathering arrests show how ordinary social events become enforcement occasions.

Transgender residents report fear of the cross-dressing proposals reported by Reuters in September 2022, which shapes how they dress in public even where the proposals' legislative status is unsettled.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public have been enacted remains unresolved; the sources available here report the proposals and the fear they caused but do not record a resulting statute.

No Taraba-specific statute, enforcement incident, or killing is documented in the sources assembled for this record. The assessment rests on the national framework and on national-level findings, with Ibadan and Lagos cited only as illustrations of the wider pattern.

The sources note that Taraba is not named among the states that have adopted Sharia, but they do not enumerate which states have, so the precise boundary of Sharia application around Taraba is not sourced here.

Whether prison placement between male and female sections is governed by written policy for pre-trial detainees or foreign nationals is not sourced; the Bobrisky coverage indicates discretion rather than a stated rule.

Taraba-specific data on access to gender-affirming care, ID document marker changes, and facilities is not present in the inventory and is not asserted here.
